summary: In days when judges judged, famine in Bethlehem (house of bread), Elimelech with wife Naomi and two sons Mahlon and Chilion go to Moab. Elimelech dies, sons marry Moabite women Orpah and Ruth, then both sons die, Naomi left with daughters-in-law. She hears Lord visited people giving bread and decides return, tells daughters-in-law return to mothers' house. Orpah kisses and returns, Ruth clings: where you go I will go, your people my people, your God my God, where you die I will die. So they return to Bethlehem at beginning barley harvest.
whyItMatters: Story of loyalty (hesed) and inclusion — Moabite woman becomes ancestor of David and Jesus. Shows redemption after emptiness, and that God's people includes outsiders who cling.

context.author: Anonymous, Samuel tradition
context.audience: Israel in monarchy/post-exile reflecting on David's Moabite ancestor and inclusion
context.setting: Bethlehem to Moab to Bethlehem, famine to harvest

outline.heading: Famine — Elimelech moves from Bethlehem to Moab, dies, sons marry Moabites then die
Naomi decides return, tells daughters-in-law to return to mothers' house
Ruth's vow — where you go I will go
Return to Bethlehem — whole town stirred, call me Mara, beginning barley harvest

keyVerses.text: Ruth said, “Don’t urge me to leave you, and to return from following you, for where you go, I will go; and where you stay, I will stay. Your people will be my people, and your God my God.
keyVerses.why: Central vow — loyalty, identity shift, covenant language.

keyVerses.text: I went out full, and Yahweh has brought me home again empty. Why do you call me Naomi, since Yahweh has testified against me, and the Almighty has afflicted me?”
keyVerses.why: Naomi = pleasant, Mara = bitter — name change reflecting grief.

keyVerses.text: So Naomi returned, and Ruth the Moabitess, her daughter-in-law, with her, who returned out of the country of Moab. They came to Bethlehem in the beginning of barley harvest.
keyVerses.why: Timing matters — harvest setting up next chapters' gleaning and redemption.

questions.question: Why does Naomi tell daughters-in-law to go back? Is she pushing them away?
questions.answer: Naomi has no more sons to give in levirate marriage custom, no means to provide, no future in Judah for Moabite widows. She tells them return to mother's house — unusual, usually father's house — perhaps because mothers would arrange remarriage. It's both realistic and selfless — she has nothing to offer. Orpah's return is not villainous, it's expected. Ruth's staying is extraordinary.

questions.question: What is so important about Ruth's vow 'where you go I will go'?
questions.answer: Most famous vow in Bible, often used in weddings, originally daughter-in-law to mother-in-law. Fourfold: where you go, I go; where you lodge, I lodge; your people my people; your God my God; where you die I die and there buried; may Yahweh punish if anything but death parts us. It's conversion, immigration, loyalty pledge all at once — changing ethnicity, religion, home, burial (ancestral). Hesed — loyal lovingkindness beyond duty.

questions.question: Why does Naomi say call me Mara (bitter) not Naomi (pleasant)?
questions.answer: Naomi = pleasant/sweet. After losing husband and two sons, she says I went out full (with family) and Yahweh brought me back empty — hand of Almighty gone out against me, dealt bitterly. Mara = bitter. She attributes emptiness to Yahweh, Shaddai (Almighty). Honest lament. Townswomen had said 'Is this Naomi?' She says no longer. Later book will move back to fullness.

questions.question: Who are Moabites and why is Ruth being Moabite significant?
questions.answer: Moabites descendants of Lot, long-time enemy/neighbor of Israel, Deuteronomy 23:3 says Moabite shall not enter assembly even to tenth generation. So Ruth as Moabite is outsider, forbidden, yet becomes great-grandmother of David (4:17) and ancestor of Jesus (Matt 1:5). Story shows inclusion of outsider through loyalty, foreshadowing Gentile inclusion. Ruth is also one of few women in Matthew's genealogy.

questions.question: What does 'beginning of barley harvest' indicate?
questions.answer: Timing is theological, not just calendar: famine to harvest (emptiness to provision), barley first grain harvested in spring (March-April). Sets up next chapters where Ruth will glean in fields during barley harvest and meet Boaz. Barley harvest then wheat harvest is season of redemption and provision. Book moves from emptiness to fullness via harvest.

glossary.def: Loyal lovingkindness, steadfast love beyond duty — Ruth's clinging.
Mara = bitter, Naomi = pleasant/sweet — name change reflecting grief.
Person from Moab, east of Dead Sea, traditionally enemy of Israel, here included.
